title: Leaving Basie in 1950; Lucky Millinder and the Local 802 transfer rule
summary: Tate, waiting out the three-month union rule, is put to work by Millinder.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So now, you left the band in '50.
Uh-huh. Oh, yeah, I was telling you about -- I went to -- yeah. I got off of that.

I was in the union and I see Lucky Millinder in the union, Local 802, it was on Sixth Avenue then, so he said, "What's going on over there?" So I says, "Well, the band's breaking up." He says, "That's what I heard." He says, "What are you going to do?" I said, "I can't do anything." I says, "I got three months before I can work." You know that law, like if a musician comes in, you know, he's got to put his -- if he's like from -- if he's not a 802 musician. You can put your transfer in, you can gig every night, but not on the same job. You have to go from here -- place to place. And after three months, you can gig on the same job. After six months, you become a member.

So Lucky says, -- Lucky was tight with the union, you know. He's a big man down there. They tell me like during Christmastime, he looked like Santa Claus. He'd go into so many presents, everybody in the union got a big present from him. He didn't care anything about money. I want to tell you some things about Lucky, too, that I think you might like. He was a great man. And he says, "Well, do you want to come to work with me?" He said, "I'm working up to 845," had a hell of a band up there, Joe Wilder and Frank Galbraith and I'm just calling Jonesie , who later

played -- had a hell of a brass section, good reed section. I said, "Man, I can't go to work. I'm just putting my transfer in today." I says, "I can't work on a --" He says, "Are you interested?" I says, "Yeah, but you know what happens if they catch me, you know?" They'll tear up your card and maybe won't let you come in the union. He said, "Don't worry about it." Well, I'd heard he was big with the union people. And so I went to work that night, Gary. And I worked six weeks at the 845. Now, I don't have but about six more to go. Then we went up to Savoy and I worked two months up to Savoy, so I'm straight, you know, I can work anywhere. I've got my three months in. And I worked with Lucky's band. And then he got ready to go on the road. He was going to do a tour. So I says, "Lucky, I'm going to tell you the truth. I've done about ten years of it and I'm grateful for everything, but I just can't make this road now." And I'm going to tell you what was happening.
